main_point.en: Jesus offers us the gift of new life.

christ_connection.en: Jesus taught that new birth, not religious activity, is how a person enters the kingdom of God and receives eternal life. New birth is given from God the Father through faith in God the Son as a work of God the Spirit. Because of God’s love, we are no longer condemned because of our sin, but we have been given eternal life in Christ.

content.en:
1 Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. 
2 This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.” 
3 Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.” 
4 Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” 
5 Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God. 
6 That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. 
7 Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ 
8 The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” 
9 Nicodemus said to him, “How can these things be?” 
10 Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things? 
11 Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. 
12 If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things? 
13 No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.”

title.en: Jesus Offers Us Freedom From Condemnation

content.en:
“14 And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, 
15 that whoever believes in him may have eternal life. 
16 For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. 
17 For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him. 
18 Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. 
19 And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil. 
20 For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. 
21 But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.”
Leaders: This week, may you be reminded of God’s deep love for you (John 3:16).

“Nicodemus thought entering God’s kingdom had everything to do with physical birth. If a person was born a Jew, he would automatically have a spot in God’s kingdom. He would only be kept out if he were blasphemous or extremely wicked. But Jesus says the opposite. No matter who a person is, he is automatically kept out of God’s kingdom by his sin. He would only be let in if he were born again. If being born again isn’t a physical birth, then what is it? Jesus says it’s a spiritual birth. The Spirit of God makes a person alive and new from the inside. The new birth happens when God’s Spirit animates the human spirit, making a person alive to the things of God. It’s the total transformation of a person from the inside out.”⁹

title.en: Jesus Offers Us Freedom From Condemnation

content.en: “This illustration from the Old Testament life of Moses shows us that the cross provides a cure from the poison of sin, deliverance from the death of sin, and removal of the condemnation of sin. The words lifted up appear twice more in this Gospel (8:28; 12:32), and each time they emphasize the centrality of the cross and the message of salvation. The sin in the desert was rebellion, and Israel needed to show faith and obedience by looking to the pole (Num. 21:9).”¹⁰

“Is there a verse anywhere in the Bible more well-known and loved than this? How poignantly it states that eternal life is not earned by begging, crying, praying, working, or joining! Salvation comes as a free gift when we believe what God has said. For almost two thousand years people have been adding to the gospel.”¹¹

“Jesus has come not just for the Jews or the elect, but for the world. He has come not to save some and to condemn others, but solely for salvation. Nevertheless, condemnation does take place—not through God’s rejection of some, but by their rejection of him (v. 18). Judgment is a matter of what people do with the light, as Jesus emphasizes at the end of the first half of the Gospel (12:46-48). One’s response to Jesus is one’s judgment because Jesus is the revelation of God himself (12:49-50).”¹²

Who was Nicodemus, the man who conversed with Jesus at night? First, Nicodemus was one of the Pharisees, a group of roughly 6,000 men deeply committed to obeying and enforcing God’s law—613 commands, along with additional laws the Jews added to ensure their obedience. He likely was a member of the Sanhedrin as well—seventy men who acted as the governing body of the Jewish nation. In other words, Nicodemus had all the right credentials. He was a highly-respected, knowledgeable teacher of the law. In the Jews’ eyes, Nicodemus was the epitome of one fit for God’s kingdom, but the right credentials, even religious ones, can’t ensure a place there. This concept would’ve been foreign to Nicodemus, who believed his lineage and self-righteousness made him secure. The radical idea that neither of these mattered led to more questions and, ultimately, Jesus unraveling the mystery of the gospel for Nicodemus and for us: No one can enter or see the kingdom without looking to the Son in faith. Our best credentials are polluted by sin, so God gave His Son to keep us from perishing (John 3:16).

Regeneration takes place at the beginning of the Christian life and is the miraculous transformation, or the new birth, that takes place within an individual through the supernatural work of the Holy Spirit (John 3:3-8; Titus 3:5). It is the divine side of conversion (a person turning to Christ in repentance and faith), being the work of God within a person’s life that causes him or her to be born again, a work that human effort is unable to produce.

God, thank you for loving us and for sending your son to free us. Help us to walk in freedom instead of believing Satan’s message of condemnation. Thank you for drawing us into the light. We commit to living in the light and showing your light to the world.

question.en: Be honest: How afraid of the dark are you (1=Not at all; 10=I sleep with a light on at all times)?

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You’ll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: Do you like to sleep in total darkness or do you need some light? Why?
When do we start being afraid of the dark? Why are we?
Can you think of a time when you were afraid and getting to a source of light made you feel safe?

content.en: Many of us were afraid of the dark as children and many of us are still! We associate darkness with all sorts of scary things; much of our fear is based in the unknown. Light brings us comfort, protection, and sight. Today, we’ll see that though our flesh is drawn to darkness and sin, light gives us sight and draws us to freedom and eternal safety.

cultural_connection.en: You’ve probably messed up before and wanted to just start over. Maybe you made a horrible grade and wanted to retake a test. Maybe you gossiped about a friend, and you’d love to undo your words and the damage they caused. Maybe you sinned and did something you never thought you’d do, and you’d love to go back in time to make the right choice. In some situations, we can start over, but when it comes to our sin, we can’t. We can’t go back to the beginning and choose never to sin. Why? When Adam and Eve fell to sin, all of humanity was infected by it. We are born into a sinful world, and we can’t fix it. This may sound hopeless, but it just means that we needed someone else to fix it for us—someone never infected with sin. Jesus’s sacrifice provides something better than a second chance because, if given another chance, we’d squander it. Instead, we are reborn! When we call on Jesus for salvation, He gives us His Spirit. We are renewed, continuously covered by Jesus’s blood and no longer bound to our sin!

question.en: Have you ever wanted to ask God a question? What would you ask?

answer.en: Maybe you have always wondered why God created spiders, or maybe you’re curious about something more serious, like why a prayer wasn’t answered the way you hoped. Nicodemus had questions too, which led him to meet with Jesus at night. Maybe Nicodemus feared what other leaders would think or maybe he had some other reason for choosing night, but Nicodemus went to the source for answers. Jesus wasn’t offended; He welcomed the conversation. We naturally wonder about things we struggle to understand, but God isn’t offended when we bring our questions to Him in a search for truth.

question.en: What was Nicodemus’s opinion of Jesus? Why wasn’t it enough?

answer.en: When Nicodemus approached Jesus at night, he called Him “Rabbi”—a term that indicated respect and meant “teacher.” Nicodemus also acknowledged that God was somehow empowering Jesus to perform signs and miracles. He recognized Jesus was from God, but he didn’t understand that Jesus is God—the promised Messiah. Nicodemus’s good opinion of Jesus wasn’t enough. How does this apply to us? Many of us think highly of Jesus; we may even acknowledge that He existed. But good opinions of Him aren’t enough. We must be born again; we must confess Him as Lord and call on Him for salvation, surrendering wholly to Him.

question.en: Does the truth that you can’t be good enough to see God’s kingdom comfort you or concern you? Why?

answer.en: Leaders: Discuss Context about Nicodemus to ensure students understand his position in Jewish culture. Some of us find comfort in our religious or worldly credentials. We celebrate checking off the right boxes: We go to church; we read our Bibles; we sing in the choir; we make good decisions; we try to be honest; we don’t lie, cheat, or steal; we don’t use profanity or party; we have good morals. All of this sounds really good, doesn’t it? But if Jesus looked at a Pharisee and member of the Sanhedrin, a man who worked to know and follow God’s law his entire life, and essentially said, “Your goodness isn’t enough; you don’t qualify,” then what does He say of our goodness? Jesus looked at one of the best of the Jews and told him that he wasn’t fit to see the Father’s kingdom. But this doesn’t have to be bad news! In fact, this is the good news of the gospel. We get to see and live now as members of the kingdom because Jesus makes us worthy. He imparted His goodness to us, making us righteous with the gift of His blood! We are reborn—new creations!

title.en: Jesus Offers Us Freedom From Condemnation

question.en: Why do people sometimes doubt God’s love for them? How deep is God’s love for us?

answer.en: Human suffering is one of the biggest reasons people doubt God’s love. We wrestle with why God lets us walk through pain if He loves us. Suffering and grieving dull our understanding. God deeply loves His Son, but He allowed Him to suffer. Why? Because He loves us deeply too (3:16). God doesn’t desire for us to suffer; we can look at Eden and see God’s original design was for us to enjoy peace, perfection, and unbroken relationship with Him. Pain and suffering exist because of sin— because humans allowed the enemy to warp truth. But in His goodness, God doesn’t waste our pain. He uses it to draw us closer to Him—to remind us that this world is broken and that His only Son was broken and bruised to redeem us. God is near when we’re hurting (Ps. 34:18). If we reframe suffering as a reminder of our brokenness, then we can stand hopefully under the weight of it, knowing God has promised that all suffering has an expiration date. Instead of allowing the enemy to use our suffering, we can lean into truth.

question.en: What could you share with people who feel like God just wants to condemn them?

answer.en: We feel judged and condemned when someone points out our mistakes. Sometimes, people do have a motive to condemn us, but God’s heart is our freedom. Jesus explained that He came to redeem us, not condemn us. The truth is that our sin condemns us. God would’ve been justified in leaving us here without hope, but He came down: Jesus dwelled with us, lived like us, experienced pain, grief, and suffering. Jesus, though sinless, took the condemnation we deserved in exchange for our freedom. God desires our salvation, not our condemnation.

question.en: What does it look like for teenagers to love and choose darkness today (v. 19)?

answer.en: Our flesh craves sin; without the transforming power of the Holy Spirit, we choose darkness. Sin masks itself as fun and freedom, when really, sin is slavery. We choose things like partying, alcohol, sexual sin. We avoid light—truth—because then we’d have to make a choice: light or dark, follow God or the world. One is our freedom; one is our bondage. We feel safer crouching in the dark, but redemption is in the light— in allowing God to expose our sin and our need for Jesus.

question.en: How can you be an instrument of light in the world? What areas of your life look more like darkness than light?

answer.en: We’re conditioned to fear the dark. Even as small children, we associate darkness with scary monsters lurking and waiting for us. Jesus drew on this theme of darkness and light because we so easily identify with it. When it comes to our physical safety, we run to the light; when it comes to our sin, we crouch in the dark. We don’t want our sin exposed in the light of day because we’d experience shame, guilt, and more—we’d have to choose either to stay in the dark or to walk into the light. Jesus said believers are light in a dark world (Matt. 5:14). We live as lights when we walk according to God’s Word. This means we’ll live differently from the world. We’ll talk differently; we’ll treat others with love and forgive enemies; we’ll seek holiness instead of popularity; we’ll use language that points to Jesus instead of cutting people down; we’ll share the gospel instead of hiding our faith. If we’ve seen the light, then we must walk in the light. When we do, we lead others to freedom and show them how to leave darkness behind: by trusting the Light of the world (John 8:12).

content.en:
Raise your hand if you can be stubborn! Let’s be honest, we want to prove to ourselves and to others that we can do what we think and say we can do. We can hit that new record in the gym and crush that ACT score. Some of us struggle to realize when we need help with something. The reality is that sometimes, we need someone else to step in for us, and that’s okay.

As much as we try, we can’t purify our hearts and minds. We need help from the only One who is capable of making us new: Jesus. So, God sent His Son down to earth to cleanse our hearts and minds—to give us new life (John 3:16). The problem with the heart is that it is deeply rooted in sin, going all the way back to the beginning—with the first humans, Adam and Eve. In this week’s lesson, Jesus referenced today’s passage. God’s people lost sight of all the Lord had done for them on the journey to the promised land. God saw Israel’s complaining and rebellion and sent poisonous snakes as a painful consequence of their distrust. But let’s not miss this important part: God made a way for them to heal. Restoration could happen only if they had the faith to look up at the bronze serpent. This act probably didn’t make sense to many of them, but they had to trust what God commanded if they wanted to be healed.

This cycle repeated for most of Israel’s history: freedom, rebellion, restoration. We repeat this cycle too. God freed us from sin, but we so easily forget and wander away from Him. You may feel ashamed, embarrassed, or even afraid to approach Him. But God sees you and loves you. He grants new life to each of us, but we must look up in faith!

question.en: How have you fallen into a cycle of complaining and disobedience toward God?
How can you release those things and embrace the new life that Jesus offers?

prayer.en: Lord, forgive me for wandering from you. Thank you for loving me and forgiving me. Help me to look to you for restoration.

content.en:
Think about your favorite teachers. Maybe they were relaxed and funny. Maybe they helped you easily understand the subject they taught by keeping class fun and interesting. Maybe they gave extensions on really hard assignments. More than likely though, one reason they are your favorite is because they were approachable. They were easy to talk to because they listened. They tried to relate to what you were going through and always had your back because they wanted you to succeed. These are the great teachers.

Being approachable is one of the qualities that separates the one true God from false gods. God desires for us to come to Him; in fact, He has always made a way to be near to His people— through sacrifices, the ark of the covenant, the tabernacle, the temple, His Son, and now, through the Holy Spirit. Because God wants us to come to Him, He welcomes our struggles and questions. We saw this in the conversation between Jesus and Nicodemus in John 3. Every question Nicodemus asked drew him closer to recognizing Jesus’s identity as the Messiah. Jesus didn’t push away his questions but engaged him in conversation. Jesus revealed God’s character, and His character remains the same. When His people seek Him, God promises to respond. Jeremiah was writing to the Jews exiled in Babylon and spoke of a future, when they would be freed and return to their land. God hadn’t left them and promised that though they were exiled, He would restore them. Though we aren’t exiled in Babylon, these verses give us hope too. God desires a relationship with us, and when we seek Him, we will find Him. He isn’t hiding and wants us to find Him. Even when you feel like you’ve wandered too far from God, you can take a single step toward Him and know He will respond.

question.en: Do you view God as being approachable? Why or why not?
Where are you not being honest with God about what’s going on in your heart? Spend time in honest prayer.

prayer.en: Lord, thank you for not pushing me away when I’m struggling or asking questions. Help me to step toward you, knowing you desire an authentic relationship with me.

content.en:
We all mess up from time to time and make a wrong choice. When this happens, we face the consequences of our actions. Maybe you recently disobeyed your parents, and they grounded you or took your phone away for a few days. Hopefully, you learned a lesson and grew as a result of that wrong decision.

The reason we make poor choices is because our hearts are broken by sin. Only God can fix this problem, and He did this by sending His Son for us. Today’s passage includes a verse that is probably one of the most well-known verses in the Bible. Can you see which one it is? You probably chose John 3:16! The verse gives us hope and assurance of God’s love, but you must also read the next two verses to really get the point. If we believe in the Lord and trust in Him for salvation, we are not condemned, though we will still face consequences here on earth for our sins. But if we know Jesus, we are forgiven and set free from the bondage of sin and death.

This doesn’t mean we get a free pass to keep doing the wrong thing because we are forgiven. Our forgiveness should lead us to do the opposite because God is so good and so kind! Paul wrote, “God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance” (Rom. 2:4). When we sin against God, not only do we receive His love and forgiveness, but we also learn what it means to follow and obey Him. As we walk with Jesus, we desire Him more than sin! God’s love meets us and teaches us to desire Him. So, the next time you do the wrong thing, confess it to God, receive His love, learn from your mistake, and ask God to help you desire Him more.

question.en: How should knowing that God desires to save you and not condemn you change the way you view your sin?
What steps do you need to take to know God better and to allow him to transform your desires?

prayer.en: Lord, thank you that your love isn’t based on anything I do or don’t do but on the finished work of Jesus on the cross. May this truth change the way I live each day.

content.en:
Let’s go back to the story of Jesus and Nicodemus talking about being “born again” in John 3. Nicodemus asked questions that many of us may ask the first time we read this passage: “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?” Nicodemus thought Jesus was talking about being born again physically, but Jesus was speaking about being born again spiritually.

The apostle Paul described this later as being a “new creation.” Paul chose these words because they carry a lot of weight! Think about it: If something is new, it stands out next to other things that are old, used, broken, and worn out. It has an extra shine and glow to it. The word creation then speaks to the beginning of something. If you have surrendered your life to Jesus, then you have been made new! You are not the person you used to be. You have Him living inside of you, convicting you of sin and forgiving you, leading and guiding you, and giving you an eternal purpose and hope. As a student, living in this reality can be really hard because so many distractions are fighting for your attention. Maybe it’s the temptation to be popular and liked by everyone, to get good grades, to never lose a game, to worry about who you’re going to go to the prom with or what you’re going to do after graduation. When we remember who we are in Christ and that He has made us new, then we’ll remember that we can trust Him with all the other details of our lives. You’re a new creation—a living, breathing testimony of God’s power to transform even the worst of us into something new!

question.en: How does understanding the words “new creation” help you better understand God’s heart for you?
What steps can you take to keep distractions from harming your relationship with Jesus?

prayer.en: Lord, remind me that I’m a new creation. Help me to live in that way and not allow the distractions of the world to pull me away.

content.en:
While we create many of the distractions that pull us away from God by not prioritizing our relationship with Him, many of them are due to the darkness around us. Ever since sin entered the picture, our world has been broken. The world isn’t how God intended it to be—without sin, without sickness and pain, perfect, peaceful. One day Jesus will come back to make all things right, but until that day, we live in a dark world. Satan works hard to put lies in our minds, and the temptation to sin is everywhere.

We aren’t powerless! Not only is Jesus with us in the darkness, but He also overcame it already. So, we have a choice to make: Will we live as new creations and walk through life empowered by the Holy Spirit living within us, or will we cave to the darkness? Walking in the light means that you desire a closeness with God above anything else. You want to know Him more, align with His heart, and do what Jesus would do. Walking in the light is choosing godliness over the sin that you desperately want to commit. And it’s confessing your sin and embracing God’s grace when you do give in.

The best time to start walking in the light is each morning when you wake up. Giving God the beginning of your day will set the tone for the rest of your day. Think about your daily schedule. Once the day gets going, it doesn’t stop between school, extra activities, and maybe work. Prioritizing time with God at the beginning of your day helps you determine to walk in the light with Him, not giving darkness a chance!

question.en: How has darkness distracted you lately? How can you be more intentional about walking in the light?
What could it look like for you to consistently begin your day with God? Make a plan. Write it down!

prayer.en: Lord, I recognize the darkness and temptation to sin all around me. I desire to walk in the light, but I can’t do it alone. Help me to come to you and do what it takes to walk in the light.
